abstract: A four-root extension theorem states that a nonempty core $H$ with every $H-v$ $(k-1)$-colorable extends to a $k$-coloring of a $K_k$-free graph when all four roots have degree at least $k$ and at most $4k-4$ edges meet the roots. We prove that this abstract bound is sharp for every $k\geq7$. Our base graph is a vertex-critical eight-chromatic, $K_7$-free graph obtained by adding a triangle and an isolated root to a thirteen-vertex, vertex-critical seven-chromatic core. Every root has degree seven and exactly twenty-five edges meet the roots. Optimal core colorings correspond to the thirteen near-perfect matchings of a triangle-free odd cactus. The triangle and isolated root require matched edges in two specified induced sets, but their permitted exposed-vertex sets are disjoint. A complete join gives the claimed family for all larger $k$, preserving vertex-criticality and the exact incident-edge threshold. We contrast this obstruction with a positive matching theorem for odd-cycle bouquets: two induced-set repair requirements can always be met under an explicit vertex-cover condition, even though arbitrary two-edge matching extension may fail. A compact standard-library certificate independently checks the construction, all matchings, clique bounds and deletion colorings. At $k=9$ the witness has nineteen vertices and 123 edges, so it violates the biplanar Euler bound. The result resolves abstract sharpness and identifies an incompatibility that geometric improvements must exclude; it does not resolve the Earth–Moon problem.

title: Sharpness of four-root coloring extension through incompatible matching repairs
